en: The Shorter Exposition:
The Exposition of the Pārāyana Chapter;
The Exposition of the Questions.
11. The Exposition of the Questions of the Young Man Jaṭukaṇṇi Having heard [the teaching],
O Hero who is free from desire for sensual pleasures,
(so said the Venerable Jaṭukaṇṇi)
I have come desiring to ask one who has crossed the flood:
Speak of the state of peace, O Sahajanetta;
speak this to me, Blessed One, according to reality.
"Having heard"—having heard, having listened to, having grasped, having reflected upon, and having discerned that "the Blessed One is indeed thus:
an arahant... a Buddha, a Blessed One. Thus:
"having heard."
The Blessed One is a hero because he has conquered;

he is a hero because he possesses energy; he is a hero because he is powerful; he is a hero because he is free from poison; he is a hero because he is self-sufficient; he is a hero because he is a hero (sūra). He is a hero because he is valiant, fearless, undaunted, unafraid, not fleeing, having abandoned fear and dread, and being free from horripilation.
He is a hero because he is detached here from all evils.
Having transcended the suffering of hell, he dwells in vigor;
being vigorous and striving,
such a hero is called "one who has become thus."
"Having heard of the Hero,
'one who does not desire sensual pleasures'": in brief, there are two kinds of sensual pleasures.
There are sensual pleasures as objects and sensual pleasures as defilements...
[as before] ...these are called sensual pleasures as objects...
[as before] ...these are called sensual pleasures as defilements.
For the Buddha, the Blessed One, sense-desires as objects have been fully understood, and sense-desires as defilements have been abandoned.

Because sense-desires as objects have been fully understood and sense-desires as defilements have been abandoned, the Blessed One does not desire sense-desires, does not long for sense-desires, does not crave sense-desires, and does not yearn for sense-desires.

Those who desire sense-desires, long for sense-desires, crave sense-desires, and yearn for sense-desires—those seekers of sense-desires, possessed by passion, perceive only what is perceived through perception.
The Blessed One does not desire sensual pleasures, does not long for sensual pleasures, does not crave sensual pleasures, and does not yearn for sensual pleasures.
Therefore, the Buddha is without desire, free from desire, one who has abandoned desire, vomited out desire, released desire, relinquished desire, and renounced desire;
he is devoid of lust, free from lust, one who has abandoned lust, vomited out lust, released lust, relinquished lust, and renounced lust; he is hungerless.
"Having heard, 'The Hero has attained Nibbāna, become cool, experiencing happiness, and dwells with self become as Brahmā,' I have no further desire for the unmade.
Thus spoke the Venerable Jatukaṇṇī.
*Iti* is a word-conjunction (*padasandhi*) ... [and so on] ...
this is [an expression of] sequential order of words (*padānupubbatā*). *Āyasmā* is a term of endearment; *āyasmā* is a designation for one who possesses reverence and deference.
"Jatukaṇṇī" is the clan name, designation, appellation, and conventional term for that brahmin—
thus spoke the Venerable Jatukaṇṇī.
They have come desiring to ask about one who has transcended the flood.
"Crossing the flood": that which has crossed the flood, transcended the flood, gone beyond it—this is "crossing the flood.
"To ask": to ask, to inquire, to entreat, to request, to propitiate.
"Unwillingly they come; unwillingly they have been asked;

we have come to one who is free from desire, who has abandoned desire, vomited out desire, released desire, relinquished desire, renounced desire, who is devoid of lust, free from lust, who has cast off lust, vomited out lust, released lust, relinquished lust, and renounced lust—we have come, we have arrived, we have approached, we have reached, we have met with you."
“O Sahajanetta, speak of the state of peace, that which transcends the flood, to me who has come desiring to ask.
Peace (*santi*) is, in one sense, both peace itself and the state of peace; it is that very same deathless *nibbāna*.
That which is the stilling of all formations, the relinquishing of all acquisitions, the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation, Nibbāna.
For this was said by the Blessed One:
"Peaceful is this state, sublime is this state, namely, the stilling of all formations, the relinquishing of all acquisitions, the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation, Nibbāna."
Furthermore, in another way, those phenomena that lead to the attainment of peace, to the touching of peace, and to the realization of peace— namely,
the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right endeavors, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the noble eightfold path—
these are called the states of peace.

Speak of, declare, teach, describe, establish, reveal, analyze, clarify, and explain the state of peace, the state of refuge, the state of shelter, the state of protection, the state of fearlessness, the state of the undecaying, the state of the deathless, the state of Nibbāna. "Born with the eye" (*sahajanetta*):
here "eye" (*netta*) refers to omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutañāṇa*).

The eye of the Buddha, the Blessed One, and his state of victory both arose at the foot of the Bodhi tree at one and the same moment, neither before nor after; therefore, the Buddha is called "born with the eye."
"Speak of the state of peace, O Sahajanetta!
Tell me, Blessed One, according to reality. By "according to reality" is meant the deathless Nibbāna... [etc. ...cessation is Nibbāna.
"Blessed One" (Bhagavā) is a designation for reverence... [etc. ...it is a descriptive term based on realization, namely, "the Blessed One."
"Tell me this"—that is, speak, declare, ...
reveal; "tell me this according to reality," [said] the Blessed One.
Therefore that brahmin said:
“Having heard of the Hero who is free from desire,
(so said the Venerable Jatukaṇṇi)”
I have come desiring to ask one who has crossed the flood:
Tell me the state of peace, O Sahajanetta;
tell this to me as it truly is, Blessed One.
For the Blessed One dwells having overcome sense-desires,
like the sun, a possessor of splendor, outshining the earth with its radiance;
O you of vast wisdom, [behold] me of limited wisdom!
"Teach me the Dhamma so that I may understand it—
the relinquishing of birth and old age in this very world—
for the Blessed One dwells having overcome all sensual desires."
"Bhagavā" is a designation for reverence ... [and so on] ... it is a realization-designation, namely, "Bhagavā.
"Sensual pleasures" (kāmā): in brief, there are two kinds of sensual pleasures—sensual pleasures as objects (vatthukāmā) and sensual pleasures as defilements (kilesakāmā) ... [and so on].
These are called sensual pleasures as objects (*vatthukāmā*) … [as before] … these are called sensual pleasures as defilements (*kilesakāmā*).

Having fully understood sensual pleasures as objects, and having abandoned, overcome, mastered, overwhelmed, exhausted, and consumed sensual pleasures as defilements, the Blessed One moves, dwells, conducts himself, acts, guards, maintains, sustains, and supports [himself].
For the Blessed One moves having overcome sensual desires.
Just as the sun is called "the radiant one" because it outshines the earth with its brilliance, so too is the sun called "the radiant one.
The earth is called "the world."
Just as the sun, endowed with radiant heat, having overcome, surpassed, overspread, consumed, and scorched the earth,
having struck down all that is shrouded in darkness and dispelled the gloom,
displays light and travels through the sky, the firmament, and the path of the air— just so is the Blessed One endowed with the radiance of knowledge.
Endowed with the power of knowledge, having dispelled all the arising of volitional formations...
[and so on] ...having shattered the darkness of defilements and the gloom of ignorance, having displayed the light of knowledge, having fully understood sense-pleasures as objects,
and having abandoned, overcome, mastered, overwhelmed, exhausted, and crushed sense-pleasures as defilements, he fares along.
“He dwells, moves about, conducts himself, protects, maintains, and sustains himself—like the sun [sustaining] the earth with its heat.
“I am one of limited wisdom; I am one of vast wisdom”—thus I am one of limited wisdom, of inferior wisdom, of base wisdom, of fourfold wisdom.
You too possess great wisdom, vast wisdom, joyful wisdom, swift wisdom, sharp wisdom, and penetrative wisdom.
"Bhūri" refers to the earth.
The Blessed One is endowed with that wisdom which is like the earth—vast and extensive.
"O you of vast wisdom, explain to me, who am of limited wisdom, the Dhamma that I may understand it.

"Dhamma" refers to the holy life (*brahmacariya*) that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end; it is meaningful, well-phrased, unique, complete, and pure. It consists of the four foundations of mindfulness... [and so on].
"Explain, teach, describe, establish, reveal, analyze, clarify, and manifest Nibbāna and the path leading to Nibbāna.
Explain the Dhamma so that I may discern it, know it, understand it, recognize it, penetrate it, attain it, touch it, and realize it—
explain the Dhamma so that I may discern it."

"The complete abandoning of birth and aging right here" means: the abandoning, the subsiding, the relinquishing, the calming, the deathless Nibbāna, of birth, aging, and death right here—this is "the complete abandoning of birth and aging right here.
Thus spoke that brahmin.
“The Blessed One indeed moves about having overcome sensual desires,
like the sun, the radiant one, outshining the earth with its heat.
O you of vast wisdom, [behold] me of limited wisdom.”
"Teach me the Dhamma so that I may understand it—
the relinquishing of birth and old age in this very world.
"Subdue greed for sensual pleasures," [he said].
(Jatukaṇṇī, said the Blessed One:
Having seen renunciation as security,
whether it be grasped or relinquished, [one should not grieve].
Let there be nothing whatsoever for you;
abandon greed for sensual pleasures.
Regarding "sensual pleasures" (kāmā), in brief, there are two kinds of sensual pleasures:
There are sensual pleasures as objects and sensual pleasures as defilements...
these are called sensual pleasures as objects...
these are called sensual pleasures as defilements.
"Crave": craving is what is called "craving.
It is lust, infatuation... [as above] ...covetousness, greed, the root of unwholesomeness.
"Remove craving for sensual pleasures": remove craving for sensual pleasures; discard it, dispel it, eliminate it, bring it to an end, and cause it to cease to exist.
"Subdue greed for sensual pleasures," said the Blessed One, addressing that brahmin by his clan name, "Jatukaṇṇī.
"The Blessed One" (Bhagavā) is a designation of reverence... [as before] ...it is a descriptive term based on realization, namely, "the Blessed One."
"Jatukaṇṇī," said the Blessed One.
"Having seen renunciation as security":
renunciation means the practice of rightness, the practice of conformity, the practice that is not contrary, the practice according to the goal.
The practice in accordance with the Dhamma, the fulfillment of the precepts, guarding the doors of the sense faculties, moderation in eating, devotion to wakefulness,
mindfulness and clear comprehension, the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power,
the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, the noble eightfold path, and Nibbāna.
Having seen, perceived, weighed, scrutinized, and made manifest the path leading to Nibbāna as secure,
as protection, as a shelter, as a refuge, as one who has become a refuge, as fearless, as deathless, as the deathless, as Nibbāna—
he sees renunciation as secure.
"Acquired or relinquished":
"Acquired" means grasped, misapprehended, adhered to, clung to, and intent upon by way of craving and by way of views.
"Or relinquished" means that which is to be relinquished, abandoned, discarded, brought to an end, and made non-existent.
"Whether acquired or relinquished:

let there be nothing whatsoever for you"—that is, the 'something' (kiñcana) of lust, the 'something' of hatred, the 'something' of delusion, the 'something' of conceit, the 'something' of views, the 'something' of defilements, and the 'something' of misconduct.
Let this 'something' not exist for you; let it not arise; let it not be present; abandon it, dispel it, bring it to an end, and cause it to cease to be.
Let there be nothing whatsoever that clings to you.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
“Withdraw your greed for sensual pleasures.”
(Jatukaṇṇī, said the Blessed One:
Having seen renunciation as security,
whether it be grasped or relinquished, [one should not grieve].
“Let there be nothing whatsoever for you.
Dry up that which was before;
let there be nothing for you afterward.
If you do not grasp at the middle, you will wander in peace.
Dry up that which was in the past: this means that you should dry up those defilements that might arise with reference to past conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*).
"Dry it up! Dry it out! Dry it thoroughly! Render it seedless! Abandon it! Dispel it! Bring it to an end!
Make it non-existent!"—thus, "dry up what was before.

Alternatively, those past formations of kamma whose results have not yet ripened: dry them up, dry them out, dry them thoroughly, dry them completely; render them seedless; abandon them, dispel them, bring them to an end, make them non-existent.
"Even so, dry up that which was before.

Let there be nothing for you afterwards"—by this, "afterwards" refers to future conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*). "Nothing" (*kiñcana*) means the nothingness of lust, the nothingness of hatred, the nothingness of delusion, the nothingness of conceit, the nothingness of views, the nothingness of defilements, and the nothingness of misconduct.

"Let this nothingness not be yours": let it not exist, let it not be produced, let it not be generated, let it not be brought into being; abandon it, dispel it, bring it to an end, and cause it to cease to be.
"May you have nothing after.
"If you will not grasp in the middle"—here "in the middle" refers to present form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
You will not grasp, will not take up, will not misapprehend, will not delight in, will not rejoice over, and will not cleave to present formations by way of craving or by way of views.

"You will abandon, dispel, bring to an end, and lead to non-existence delighting, welcoming, cleaving to, grasping, misapprehending, and adhering"—if you do not seize them in the middle, you will wander at peace;
you will wander at peace because of the subsiding of lust, [and] because of the subsiding of hatred... [and so on].
"Because of the calming, the stilling, the subsiding, the quieting, the burning away, the extinguishing, the disappearance, and the allaying of all unwholesome volitional formations,
you will move, dwell, conduct yourself, behave, protect, maintain, and sustain yourself as one who is peaceful, stilled, quieted, extinguished, and allayed."
"You shall wander at peace.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
"Dry up that which was in the past..."
“Let there be nothing for you afterwards;
if you do not grasp at anything in between,
you will wander in peace.”
For one who is entirely free from greed regarding name-and-form, O Brahmin,
no taints exist within him.
"By these one escapes the power of Death.

A brahmin who is entirely free from craving for name-and-form"—here, "entirely" (*sabbaso*) means in every way, in all respects, in every manner, completely, without remainder, without residue; this word "entirely" denotes total exhaustion.
"Name" refers to the four formless aggregates.
"Form" refers to the four great elements and the form derived from the four great elements.
"Greed" is a term for craving.
Whatever lust, infatuation, ... [as above] ... covetousness, greed, and unwholesome root there is—[for one who is] entirely free from craving for name-and-form, O Brahmin:

for one who is entirely free from craving, devoid of craving, abandoned of craving, removed of craving, released from craving, relinquished of craving, and has cast off craving; for one who is free from lust."
"For one who is free from lust, who has abandoned lust, who has vomited out lust, who is released from lust, who has relinquished lust,
and who has renounced lust— for such a one, O Brahmin, who is entirely devoid of craving for name-and-form,
the taints do not exist."
"Outflows" (āsava) refers to the four outflows:
the outflow of sensual desire, the outflow of existence, the outflow of views, and the outflow of ignorance.
"For one who has" refers to the Arahant whose outflows are exhausted.

"They do not exist" means that these taints do not exist for him, they are not present, they are not found, they are not obtained; they have been abandoned, cut off, stilled, subsided, rendered incapable of arising, and burnt up by the fire of knowledge—thus, "the taints do not exist for him.

By which taints one would fall under the power of death, or by which taints one might come under the power of death, or come under the power of Māra, or come under the power of the faction of Māra—[those taints do not exist for him].
Those taints do not exist for him; they are not present, are not found, and are not obtained. They have been abandoned, cut off, stilled, and calmed;
incapable of arising again, they are burnt by the fire of knowledge—those through which one would fall under the power of death.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
“Completely free from greed for name-and-form, O brahmin,
his taints do not exist.”
“By which one does not fall into the power of Death. At the conclusion of the verse... [as before] ...
“The Blessed One is my Teacher, venerable sir; I am his disciple.”
The eleventh exposition: The Questions of the Young Brahmin Jaṭukaṇṇi.
